Buy it if…

  • You're starting from zero — a drill/driver kit is the correct first tool, full stop.
  • You want one battery family for the drill, the yard tools and the work light.
  • You'll hang, build, assemble and repair things a few times a month.

Skip it if…

  • You already own batteries from another platform — buy that brand's bare tool instead and save $80+.
  • Your only job is flat-pack furniture twice a year — a $40 12V driver is honestly enough.
  • You're tempted by a no-name 47-piece mega-kit. The drill is fine; the bits are not.
The verdict

New to cordless? Start with Ryobi ONE+ and spend the savings on a second battery. Already know you'll use it weekly for years? DeWalt 20V MAX. Build decks and drive lags for fun? Milwaukee M18 FUEL. Whatever you pick — commit to the platform.

What actually matters

Brushless motor. More power, longer runtime, longer life. Worth it if the price gap is under ~$50; not a dealbreaker on a budget kit.

Two batteries, minimum. One on the tool, one on the charger. A kit with a single 1.5Ah battery will frustrate you by the second project. Look for 2.0Ah packs or better.

Chuck size. 1/2-inch metal chuck grips real bits. 3/8-inch plastic chucks are for light duty only.

Weight in hand. You'll hold this over your head into a ceiling joist someday. A compact drill you control beats a monster you wrestle.

FAQs

Drill/driver vs impact driver — which first?A drill/driver. It drills holes and drives screws. An impact driver is the better screw-driving tool, but it's the second purchase, not the first.
Is 12V enough?For furniture assembly and light hanging, yes. For deck screws, drilling studs and mixing anything, go 18V/20V.
When do these go on sale?Holiday weekends and Black Friday are when platform kits drop hardest — the same sale pattern that took 40% off my solar batteries.

Still gas? A basic gas mower (~$199–299) — best for thick, tall, or wet grass on a budget. If you regularly let the yard go and mow it down wet, gas torque and a $200 price tag still make sense. You'll pay it back in maintenance time.

Buy electric if…

  • Your yard is under ~1/4 acre and you mow most weeks.
  • Garage space is tight — most electrics fold and stand upright.
  • You're done with pull cords, oil, plugs and stale gas.

Stick with gas if…

  • Your lot is bigger, sloped, or the grass is routinely tall and wet.
  • You already own a good gas mower that runs — run it till it dies, then switch.
  • You need to mow for 90+ minutes straight without a battery swap.
The verdict

Small yard, normal grass: EGO 56V if the budget allows, Greenworks if it doesn't. The real cost isn't the mower — it's the batteries — so buy into the yard platform you'll also use for your trimmer and blower, and get the kit with the bigger battery, not the bare tool.

What actually matters

Battery size (Ah) is runtime. A 5.0Ah pack mows a typical small yard; 7.5Ah gives you slack for thick spring growth. Two smaller batteries beat one if you also run a trimmer.

Deck size. 20–21 inches is the sweet spot for small yards — wide enough to finish fast, narrow enough to store and maneuver.

Self-propelled? On a flat small yard, it's weight and cost you don't need. On any slope, it's worth every penny.

Storage. Fold-flat handles and upright storage are the hidden feature you'll appreciate every single week in a small garage.

FAQs

How long does a battery mower actually run?Roughly 35–60 minutes per charge depending on battery size and grass thickness — enough for most yards under 1/4 acre in one go.
Can one battery run my mower and trimmer?Yes, if you stay in one platform and voltage line (EGO 56V, Greenworks 40V, Ryobi 40V). That's the whole point of picking a platform.
What about winter storage?Store batteries indoors, around half charge, out of the freezing garage if you can. Heat and deep-freeze storage are what kill them early.

Watts (W) — can it run it?

  • Watts are power right now — what the inverter can push at once.
  • A fridge draws ~100–200W running (with a startup surge). A sump pump can surge past 1,000W.
  • If the appliance's watts beat the station's watts, it won't run. Period.

Watt-hours (Wh) — for how long?

  • Watt-hours are fuel in the tank — total stored energy.
  • Runtime ≈ Wh ÷ appliance watts. 1,000Wh ÷ a 150W fridge ≈ 6+ hours of actual run time (fridges cycle on and off, so real-world is longer).
  • This is the number to shop by. A "2,000W" station with 500Wh is a sprinter, not backup.
The verdict

Size by watt-hours first, watts second. For fridge + phones + lights through an outage, ~1,000Wh is the honest starting point. And learn from my build below: buy the battery once. A 288Wh box won't grow into a 2,000Wh one — an expandable system will. Use the sizer tool right under this guide to run your own numbers.

What actually matters

LiFePO4 battery chemistry. The newer lithium-iron-phosphate packs last 3,000+ cycles — roughly a decade of outages — versus ~500–800 for older lithium-ion. For a buy-it-once garage box, this is the spec that matters most.

Solar input. If you'll charge from panels, check the max solar watts and connector type. 200–400W of panel keeps a 1–2kWh station topped up on a sunny day.

Pass-through / UPS mode. Some units can sit between the wall and your fridge and switch over automatically when the power drops. That's the garage-friendly way to run one.

Weight honesty check. 1,000Wh is roughly 25–30 lbs. 2,000Wh is 45–60 lbs. "Portable" gets relative fast — know where it'll live.

FAQs

Can it run my whole house?No — that's a different animal. A portable station covers essentials for hours. Whole-house backup is a fixed system like mine below: 48V, 25 kWh, and a 12,000W-class inverter.
Power station or gas generator?Station for quiet, indoor-safe, zero-maintenance backup of essentials. Gas generator for multi-day outages and big loads — at the cost of noise, fuel and never running it in the garage.
When should I buy?Black Friday and Prime Day are when this category discounts hardest — I got 40% off my server-rack batteries on a Black Friday deal. Patience is a spec.

Best Gas Generator for Home Backup: Inverter vs. Conventional, Sized Right

Running watts vs. starting watts

  • Running watts are what the generator sustains — the steady load.
  • Starting watts are the 2–3 second surge when a motor starts. A fridge compressor or well pump can surge to 3–4× its running watts.
  • Size by starting watts: add the starting watts of the biggest motor to the running watts of everything else running at the same time.
  • Worked example — fridge + lights: fridge 150W running / ~600W starting + LED lights 60W + phone chargers 20W + chest freezer 100W running / ~500W starting = ~330W running, ~1,180W starting. A 2,200W inverter generator covers it with room to spare.
  • Worked example — well pump: a 1 HP well pump draws ~1,000W running and surges to 3,000–4,000W starting. Add a fridge and lights and you need ~4,500W of starting power — the 4,500W inverter class at minimum, or the 12,000W DuroMax above for comfort.

Inverter vs. conventional

  • Inverter generators vary engine speed with load, so they sip fuel, run quiet (48–61 dBA), and make clean sine-wave power under 3% THD — safe for laptops, TVs, and solar inverters.
  • Conventional open-frame generators run at a fixed 3,600 RPM: louder, thirstier, and their voltage and frequency wander as the load changes. Fine for heaters, saws, and incandescent lights — rough on sensitive electronics.
  • For a house, the inverter is the default pick. Buy conventional only when you need big watts cheap and the loads are dumb.
  • Parallel capability: most inverters in this guide pair with a second identical unit (or a companion model) through a parallel kit, doubling output. It is the cheapest way to grow from 2,200W to 3,600W without selling the first machine.
The verdict

Size by starting watts, not the headline number. For most homes the 4,500W inverter class is the sweet spot — it starts a well pump or a big freezer and still sips fuel. Buy the smallest inverter that covers your biggest motor plus the essentials, keep a conventional only for big dumb loads, and never run any of them in the garage — that rule has no exceptions.

Pairing a generator with solar batteries: do you need a chargeverter?

If you run a solar + battery system like mine — 48V, 25 kWh across five 100Ah server-rack batteries behind an EG4 12000XP — the generator question changes. You are not running loads off the generator. You are refilling the bank, and the bank is what runs the house. That is what a chargeverter is for.

A chargeverter is an AC-to-DC battery charger that sits between the generator and the battery bank. Generator AC goes in, clean DC charging comes out, straight to the bank — and the inverter never sees the generator’s power at all. That matters because a conventional generator’s voltage and frequency wander as the load changes, and the electronics in a modern solar inverter are sensitive to that. Feed one straight into the inverter’s AC input and it may refuse to charge, throw faults, or take damage over time. The chargeverter takes the dirty power so the inverter doesn’t have to.

When you need one: you have a 24V or 48V solar battery bank and a conventional or open-frame generator; you want to refill a big bank fast during a multi-day outage (a 100-amp chargeverter pushes about 5 kW into the bank); or your inverter’s generator input is fussy about power quality.

When you don’t: your generator is an inverter generator — it already makes clean, stable power and works directly with solar inverters, no chargeverter needed. That is one more reason the four inverter picks above are the right pairing for a solar home. You also don’t need one if you have no battery bank at all — just run the loads straight off the generator.

Size it to the generator: a 100-amp chargeverter at 240V pulls up to about 5.8 kW, so it wants a 6,500W-class generator at full tilt — but both picks below let you dial the charge current down to match a smaller machine. On 120V input the output is lower (the ECO-WORTHY gives up to 60A, the EG4 up to 50A), so full power needs a 240V outlet.

The EG4 Chargeverter is 48V only — it will not charge a 24V bank. If you run 24V, the same job needs a 24V AC-to-DC charger sized to your bank (a 40-amp charger suits a 100Ah bank), matched to your battery chemistry: a LiFePO4 charger is not a lead-acid charger.

What actually matters

Fuel and runtime. Gasoline goes stale in months — use ethanol-free gas with stabilizer and rotate the can every season, or run dual-fuel on propane, which stores indefinitely. A 20-pound propane tank runs a 4,500W inverter for up to 21 hours at a quarter load.

Noise. Decibels are measured at 23–25 feet: 52 dBA is conversation level, 61 dBA is a normal voice raised, 74 dBA is a loud vacuum. Every 10 dBA roughly doubles the perceived loudness — the gap between an inverter and an open-frame is the gap between a conversation and a lawn mower.

Parallel capability. Most inverters in this guide pair with a second identical unit (or a companion model) through a parallel kit, doubling output. It is the cheapest way to grow from 2,200W to 3,600W without selling the first machine.

Carbon monoxide — the rule that matters most. Never run a generator in the garage, basement, porch, or near an open window or door — not even with the door open. Twenty feet from the house, exhaust pointed away, and a battery CO alarm in the house. CO is odorless, and the garage is where people die from it.

Never backfeed. Do not plug a generator into a wall outlet to “feed the house” — it energizes the lines outside and can kill a lineman. Run extension cords to the loads, or have an electrician install a transfer switch or interlock kit.

Break-in and maintenance. Change the oil after the first 20–25 hours, then per the manual. Run the machine under load for 20 minutes every month or two so the carburetor stays clean and you know it starts.

FAQs

Power station or gas generator?Station for quiet, indoor-safe, zero-maintenance backup of essentials — see Guide 03. Gas generator for multi-day outages and big loads like a well pump, at the cost of noise, fuel, and never running it in the garage.
Can a generator run my whole house?A portable generator plus a transfer switch runs your essential circuits — fridge, freezer, well pump, some lights. True whole-house backup is a standby generator or a fixed solar + battery system like mine: 48V, 25 kWh, and a 12,000W-class inverter.
Can I plug a generator into my solar inverter?Only if the inverter accepts it. A conventional generator’s wandering voltage is rough on sensitive inverter electronics — that is exactly what the chargeverter section above is for. An inverter generator’s clean power works directly.
How much fuel should I keep?A 5-gallon can is roughly a day of moderate-load runtime on a 4,500W inverter. Keep two cans rotated, or a 20-pound propane tank if your generator is dual-fuel — propane never goes stale.

My take on each one — verdict, buy it, skip it

Chainsaw, 18″ rear-handle — ECHO DCS-5000 · Verdict: Start here.This is the lead pick for a reason. It handles firewood, downed limbs and storm cleanup around the house without the gas-saw ritual of mixing fuel and fighting a pull cord in January. Buy it if you heat with wood, clean up after storms, or take down the occasional tree. Skip it if your only cutting is a Christmas tree once a year — borrow one instead.
Chainsaw, top-handle — ECHO DCS-2500T · Verdict: The specialist.A top-handle saw is a pruning tool, not a firewood tool — it's built for limbing and work in the tree, and it's light enough to control all day. Buy it if you prune regularly or already own the rear-handle saw and want its partner. Skip it if you're buying your first and only chainsaw — get the 18″ rear-handle DCS-5000 first, every time.
String trimmer — ECHO DSRM-2600 · Verdict: The one you'll use most.Of everything on this list, the trimmer earns its keep weekly. It has the power for thick edges, not just wispy grass, and it shares its battery with the blower you'll grab right after. Buy it if you trim more than a postage-stamp yard. Skip it if you're already deep in another battery platform — stay in your system.
Blower — ECHO DPB-2500 · Verdict: Quiet, instant, done.Blowing off the driveway and garage floor goes from a chore to a two-minute habit when the tool starts instantly and lives on the same charger as everything else. Buy it if you have concrete, a garage, or trees — so, basically, a house. Skip it if fall leaves are your main event on a big lot; a backpack blower (gas or the biggest battery you can get) still wins that one specific fight.
Hedge trimmer — ECHO DHC-2300 · Verdict: The one I didn't know I needed.I put this purchase off the longest and regretted waiting. Hedges that took an afternoon of hand-shearing and a corded trimmer take an hour, cleanly. Buy it if you have hedges or foundation shrubs you shape more than once a year. Skip it if your whole shrub count is two boxwoods — hand shears are honestly fine there.
Mower — ECHO DLM-2100SP · Verdict: Buy it for the platform.On its own it's a solid 21″ self-propelled mower. In this lineup it's better than that: it runs on the same 56V batteries as your saw, trimmer and blower, so your spare packs are never sitting idle. Buy it if you're building the ECHO yard and your lot is small-to-medium. Skip it if your yard is big, steep or regularly overgrown — that's still heavy-duty mower territory, and no battery mower will love it.

Buy the ECHO lineup if…

  • You want one 56V battery system for the whole yard — saw, trimmer, blower, hedges and mower.
  • You're done with mixing gas, stale fuel and pull cords that fail on the coldest day.
  • You trust a brand pros have run for decades and want that build quality in battery form.

Skip it if…

  • You're already invested in another yard platform (EGO, Ryobi 40V, Greenworks) — switching costs you a second set of batteries for no real gain.
  • You run a crew or cut commercially all day — runtime-per-charge still favors gas for nonstop work.
  • You only need one tool, once — a single bare tool from whatever platform you already own is the cheaper honest answer.
The verdict

I own this lineup and I'd buy it again — starting with the 18″ DCS-5000 chainsaw, then the trimmer and blower, then the rest as the yard demands. The tools are good; the single 56V battery platform underneath all of them is the real recommendation. One charger wall, a few packs, every yard job covered.

What actually matters

Buy batteries with the tools, not after. Kits that bundle a 56V pack and charger are almost always cheaper than bare tools plus a battery later. Two packs is the working minimum — one running, one charged.

Rear-handle first, top-handle second. A top-handle saw is a specialist pruning tool with a different balance and safety profile. For ground work and firewood, the 18″ rear-handle is the correct — and safer — default.

Chains still need care. Battery power ends gas maintenance, not bar oil, chain sharpening or tension checks. Budget for a spare chain and a file; a sharp chain is the difference between a saw that cuts and a saw that fights you.

Store the packs right. Same rule as my solar batteries: indoors, around half charge for long storage, out of the deep freeze. Treat the packs well and the platform lasts for years.

FAQs

Do all of these really use the same battery?Yes — the whole lineup here is ECHO's 56V eFORCE platform. A pack from the trimmer kit runs the chainsaw, the blower, the hedge trimmer and the mower. That's the point of the lineup.
Can a battery chainsaw really replace a gas one?For homeowner work — firewood, cleanup, pruning, small-to-medium trees — yes, in my experience it has. For all-day commercial felling, gas still has a runtime edge. Know which user you are.
Which one should I buy first?The job you do most. For most people that's the trimmer; if wood and storm cleanup are your reality in Pekin, it's the 18″ chainsaw. Either way, the kit with the battery is the right first purchase — everything after it can be a bare tool.

Prices are approximate November 2026 ranges for kits with battery and charger where bundled — always re-check the current price before buying, as ECHO gear moves a lot around holiday sales.

Buy a kit if…

  • You're starting from zero — a kit is the cheapest honest way to start a battery platform, and the platform is the real purchase.
  • You want two batteries from day one: one in the tool, one on the charger.
  • The tool is a saw, blower or mower — those want a 4.0Ah or bigger pack in the box, not bought later.

Skip the kit if…

  • You already own batteries on a platform — buy that platform's bare tool instead and save the battery money.
  • The listing is the bare-tool version in disguise — check the model number (kit versions usually end in K, P1 or C2, or say 'kit' in the title).
  • One small battery across five tools is the deal — one battery shared by a combo kit means a lot of waiting.
The verdict

If you are starting from zero, buy the platform first and the tool second. For workshop tools, the DeWalt DCK240C2 drill + impact kit ($149–$179) is the cheapest honest start, and the Milwaukee 3697-22 ($399) is the buy-once pick. For the yard, the EGO ST1623T trimmer and LB6504 blower kits put you on the strongest battery yard platform, and the ECHO DCS-5000 chainsaw kit shares its battery with the whole ECHO 56V eFORCE lineup Josh runs himself. Whatever you buy, buy the kit — the battery and charger in the box are worth more than the discount looks like.

What actually matters

Battery platform. the platform is the real purchase. Ryobi ONE+ has 300+ tools and the lowest prices. DeWalt 20V MAX and Milwaukee M18 have the deepest pro ranges. EGO 56V is the strongest yard platform. ECHO 56V eFORCE is the one Josh runs himself. Pick one platform per job type and stay on it — batteries do not swap between brands.

Amp-hours (Ah). Ah is the fuel tank. A 2.0Ah pack is fine for a drill; a saw, blower or mower wants 4.0Ah or more. Two small batteries beat one big one for drills; one big battery beats two small ones for saws.

Charger speed. a standard charger takes 60–90 minutes for a 5.0Ah pack. A rapid charger does it in 30–45 minutes. If the kit ships a rapid charger, that is worth real money — it is in the pick notes above.

Kit vs bare tool. always check the model number. Kit versions usually end in K, P1, C2, or say 'kit' in the title. The bare-tool version of the same tool can look identical in a listing — and cost you another $100+ in batteries.

FAQs

Do I need the same brand for all my tools?No — but every new platform means new batteries and a new charger, so most people settle on one platform for workshop tools and one for yard tools.
Is a bigger battery always better?For runtime, yes. For weight, no — a 5.0Ah pack on a drill makes it heavy overhead. Match the battery to the job.
Can I use a 20V battery in a 60V tool?No — unless it is a FLEXVOLT battery, which is designed to switch voltages. Regular 20V MAX packs do not fit 60V tools.
How long do lithium batteries last?Years with normal use. Store them indoors, do not leave them flat for months, and do not charge a frozen pack.
Why do some kits only include one battery?Cost. One battery keeps the box price down. For a drill that is fine; for a saw or blower, plan on a second pack.

Prices are approximate November 2026 ranges for kits with battery and charger — several are Black Friday / sale prices that will move, so re-check the current price before buying.

Tools · Guide 07

Best hand tool sets for a home garage

Power tools get the attention, but hand tools do most of the work in a home garage. A socket set, a wrench set, a pliers set and a screwdriver set will handle nearly everything that is not a cut or a hole — and unlike a battery platform, a good hand tool set never goes obsolete. The trick is buying a set instead of single tools one emergency at a time. A set costs less per tool, every piece has a home in the case, and you stop discovering at 9 PM that you own three 10 mm sockets and no 12 mm.

This guide is a research roundup, not a hands-on test. Picks are drawn from 2026 roundups and retailer listings checked in November 2026. Where roundups disagreed — most often on exact prices — the range shown is the honest spread, and anything we could not confirm as a complete set is listed separately at the end rather than presented as a pick.

As an Amazon Associate, ShedWorks earns from qualifying purchases.

Quick picks — Socket sets

The single most useful thing you can put in a home garage. Buy 6-point sockets when you can — they grip the flats of a bolt instead of the corners, so they round off fewer fasteners. Chrome vanadium steel is the standard; chrome-moly (Cr-Mo) is the tougher choice for impact use.

The verdict

If you are starting from an empty toolbox, buy in this order:

1. CRAFTSMAN 230-Piece Mechanics Tool Set (CMMT45306) — the one case that covers sockets, wrenches and hex keys for most cars and home jobs.

2. TEKTON 15-Piece Combination Wrench Set (18772) — the wrenches you will reach for every day, if the mechanics set's wrenches aren't enough.

3. IRWIN VISE-GRIP GrooveLock 2-Piece Set (2078709) — the best-value pliers buy in this guide, under $30.

4. CRAFTSMAN 8-Piece Bi-Material Screwdriver Set (CMHT65075N) — the standard home screwdriver set.

5. Bondhus 22-Piece Ball End L-Wrench Double Pack (20399) — hex keys for furniture, bikes and appliances.

If you already own the basics, the single best upgrade in this guide is the KNIPEX Cobra 3-piece set — it is the tool you will notice every time you pick it up. And if you want one set that does everything, the DeWalt 247-piece mechanics set is the buy-it-for-life pick.

What actually matters

Steel. Steel type: chrome vanadium is the standard for sockets and wrenches; S2 steel is better for hex keys and bits; chrome-moly (Cr-Mo) is the pick for impact use.

Points. 6-point beats 12-point for sockets: it grips the flats of a bolt, so it rounds off fewer fasteners. 12-point is fine for wrenches, where access matters more.

Ratchet teeth. Ratchet teeth: 72 teeth means a 5-degree swing; 84 or 90 teeth means 4 degrees. More teeth = less swing room needed in tight spots.

Warranty. Warranty: TEKTON, Craftsman, GearWrench and Bondhus all offer lifetime warranties. A lifetime warranty on a $30 set is worth more than a 1-year warranty on a $100 set.

Piece count. Piece count lies: a 228-piece set and a 69-piece set can hold almost the same number of usable sockets — the extra pieces are hex keys, bits and screwdrivers you may already own twice over. Count sockets, not pieces.

Case. Case: a set that lives in a labeled case gets used; a set in a bag gets lost. Check that the case closes properly and the latches hold.

SAE vs metric. SAE vs metric: American cars and older homes are SAE; imports, bikes and modern appliances are metric. Most garages need both.

FAQs

Do I need both SAE and metric?Yes, for most garages. American vehicles and older homes use SAE (inches); imports, bicycles and modern appliances use metric. A set that covers both costs little more than a single-system set.
What is the difference between a socket set and a mechanics tool set?A socket set is sockets, ratchets and extensions only. A mechanics tool set adds combination wrenches and often pliers, screwdrivers and hex keys. If you own nothing, buy the mechanics set; if you own wrenches already, buy the socket set.
Are cheap tool sets worth it?For occasional home use, yes — a $30–$50 set from a known brand handles most jobs. For daily or trade use, cheap steel rounds off fasteners and wears out. Buy the best set you can afford for the tools you use most, and go budget on the ones you use twice a year.
What does 6-point vs 12-point mean?A 6-point socket contacts all six flats of a hex bolt, so it grips better and rounds off fewer fasteners. A 12-point socket fits in tighter spots and works on 12-point fasteners, but grips less. For sockets, 6-point is the safer default.
Do these sets work on my car?The socket and mechanics sets in sections 1 and 2 cover most cars and trucks — they include both SAE and metric sizes across 1/4", 3/8" and 1/2" drives. Check your vehicle's common fastener sizes first; some European cars need Torx and E-Torx sockets, which are not in these sets.

Gas vs battery: which one do you actually need?

Josh runs the ECHO 56V eFORCE battery lineup himself — the DCS-5000 and DCS-2500T chainsaws, trimmer, blower, hedge trimmer and mower — and recommends them in our ECHO battery yard tools guide. For most jobs around the house, battery wins: no fuel mixing, no pull cord, no fumes, and quiet enough to run early in the morning. A 56V battery saw with a 4–5 Ah battery handles limbing, storm cleanup and a surprising amount of firewood.

Gas still wins when the work is big and the day is long. A gas saw runs as long as you keep feeding it fuel, pulls a longer bar, and costs less per unit of power at the top end — a CS-590 with a 24-inch bar costs about the same as a top battery saw kit and will out-cut it all day. The honest rule: if you cut a cord or less a year, go battery. If you heat with wood, fell trees, or run a saw for hours at a time, get a gas saw — and keep a battery saw for the quick jobs.

Safety gear: don't skip this

A chainsaw is the most dangerous tool in this guide, and the gear is not optional. At minimum: chainsaw chaps (they stop the chain on contact with your leg), a helmet with face screen and hearing protection, gloves, and steel-toe boots. Add a first-aid kit with a tourniquet to the truck or the wood pile. Never cut alone if you can avoid it, never cut above shoulder height, and keep the chain sharp — a dull chain is what causes kickback and fatigue.See the full kit in our chainsaw safety gear and firewood tools guide.

Buy a gas saw if…

  • You heat with wood, clear storm damage, or fell a few trees a year — the work runs all day and a gas saw has no runtime clock.
  • You pull a 20-inch bar through hardwood and need power a battery saw can't match at the price.
  • You want the most engine per dollar — a CS-590 with a 24-inch bar costs about the same as a top battery saw kit and out-cuts it all day.

Skip it if…

  • You cut a cord or less a year — go battery. Josh runs the ECHO 56V eFORCE lineup himself for exactly those quick jobs.
  • Your cutting is limbing and storm cleanup — a 56V battery saw with a 4–5 Ah battery handles it, with no fuel mixing or pull cord.
  • You want to buy a STIHL online — STIHL sells through dealers only; buy from a dealer for the warranty and support.
The verdict

Buy the ECHO CS-400 if you want one gas saw for a normal property — it is the best homeowner saw in this guide. Buy the ECHO CS-590 Timber Wolf if you heat with wood and want the most power for the money. Buy the Husqvarna 450 Rancher if you want the best all-rounder with the strongest dealer network. And if you already run the ECHO 56V battery lineup like Josh does, the gas saw is your second saw for the big days — not your first saw for the quick jobs.

What actually matters

Engine size (cc) matched to the bar. 40 cc drives 16–18 in, 50 cc drives 18–20 in, 60 cc drives 20–24 in. A bar that is too long for the engine bogs down and wears the saw out.

Weight matters more than horsepower. you carry the saw all day, and a 13 lb saw feels very different from a 10 lb saw after an hour.

Easy starting. look for a decompression valve or a reduced-effort starter (ECHO i-30, Husqvarna Smart Start).

Adjustable oiler. worth having on saws 50 cc and up, so you can feed more oil to a long bar.

Dealer and parts support. ECHO, Husqvarna and STIHL all have dealer networks; budget brands are harder to get parts for.

Fuel. all of these run on a 50:1 gas-to-oil mix (89 octane or higher). Use ethanol-free fuel if you can get it, and never store mixed fuel for months.

FAQs

Do I need a gas saw if I already own a battery saw?Only if you cut a lot. A good 56V battery saw covers limbing, storm cleanup and light firewood. Gas earns its keep at several cords a year or on trees over 18 inches across.
How big a bar do I need?The bar should be at least as long as the thickest log you cut regularly. For most homeowners that is 16–18 inches. A 20-inch bar is for serious firewood; 24 inches is for felling.
Can I buy a STIHL on Amazon?No. STIHL sells through authorized dealers only. Any Amazon listing is a third-party reseller — buy from a dealer for the warranty and support.
How often do I sharpen the chain?Every tank of fuel is a good rule of thumb for firewood work, and immediately if you hit dirt, a nail, or the chain starts throwing dust instead of chips.

The best-known homestead bandsaw mills are sold factory-direct, not on Amazon. We are not pretending otherwise — here is what they cost and where to get them, so the guide stays honest:

  • Woodland Mills HM126 / HM126MAX — ~$3,399–$4,665, 26 in log diameter, up to 14 HP. The original Woodland Mills sawmill and the homestead favourite. Buy direct at woodlandmills.com.
  • Woodland Mills HM130MAX — ~$4,000–$5,000, 30 in log diameter. The wide-capacity step up. Buy direct at woodlandmills.com.
  • Norwood LumberPro HD36 / HD36v2 — ~$6,500–$9,500, 36 in log diameter, 13 ft log length, 16–23 HP Briggs & Stratton. A heavy-duty portable bandsaw mill. Buy direct at norwoodsawmills.com.
  • Wood-Mizer LT15 — ~$5,000–$10,000+, the premium portable mill. Buy direct at woodmizer.com.

Rule of thumb from the roundups: a chainsaw mill is enough if you cut a few beams or slabs a year. A bandsaw mill starts making financial sense once you expect to saw hundreds or thousands of board feet — at roughly $1–$3 saved per board foot over buying lumber, a $3,000 mill pays for itself around 1,000–3,000 board feet.

Buy it if…

  • You have trees on your own land to turn into lumber, firewood and mulch — instead of paying someone else to haul them away.
  • You'll actually mill hundreds of board feet — at roughly $1–$3 saved per board foot over buying lumber, a $3,000 bandsaw mill pays for itself around 1,000–3,000 board feet.
  • You burn several cords a winter — that's when a gas splitter earns its price over an electric one.

Skip it if…

  • You mill a few beams or slabs a year — a chainsaw mill attachment under $300 is enough; a bandsaw mill is money sitting still.
  • You expect the big name-brand mills on Amazon — Woodland Mills, Norwood and Wood-Mizer are sold factory-direct, not on Amazon.
  • You chip mostly green wood with an electric chipper — dry wood chips far better, and anything over ~1.75 inches needs gas.
The verdict

Start with the chainsaw mill: a Granberg Alaskan MKIV for about $260–$305 turns a saw you already own into a mill, and it pays for itself in a few hundred board feet. If you burn wood, the WEN 56208 electric splitter at about $335 is the best value in the whole guide, and the Sun Joe CJ603E at about $200 is the chipper to buy if you chip near the house. The big bandsaw mills are real money — $2,500 to $10,000 — and they only make sense if you will actually mill hundreds or thousands of board feet. Buy the machine for the wood you have, not the wood you wish you had.

What actually matters

Sawmills. Chainsaw mills are cheap and slow and waste more wood per cut than a bandsaw blade — but they cost a tenth of a bandsaw mill. Bandsaw mills are faster and thinner-kerfed, but they need a flat site, blade stock, and real money. Buy the mill that matches how many board feet you will actually cut, not the one you dream about.

Log splitters. Tonnage is only half the story — cycle time is the other half. A 7-ton electric with a 9-second cycle can out-split a 25-ton gas machine on straight-grained wood, but only gas handles green, knotty rounds. Horizontal/vertical operation matters: vertical mode saves your back on big rounds.

Wood chippers. Match the max branch diameter to your actual brush — electric chippers top out around 1.75 inches, and feeding anything bigger just jams them. Dry wood chips far better than green wood in any electric chipper. Gas chippers take 3-inch branches but are loud, heavy and need maintenance.

FAQs

Can I really buy a sawmill on Amazon?A chainsaw mill attachment, yes — Granberg, VEVOR and Zozen all sell on Amazon, and one real bandsaw mill (MechMaxx 26-inch) has a live Amazon listing. The big name-brand bandsaw mills (Woodland Mills, Norwood, Wood-Mizer) are sold direct from the manufacturer, not on Amazon.
Do sawmills ship free?Chainsaw mill attachments ship like normal Amazon orders. Full bandsaw mills ship freight — expect a pallet delivery, possible liftgate fees, and assembly time. Check the listing's shipping terms before you order.
Electric or gas log splitter?Electric for 1–2 cords of seasoned wood: quieter, cleaner, cheaper, no engine to maintain. Gas for 3+ cords, green wood, or knotty hardwood — nothing electric keeps up with a 25-ton gas machine.
What size chipper do I need?Measure the thickest branches you actually chip. Under 1.75 inches, an electric chipper is fine. Over 2 inches, you need gas.

Prices are approximate November 2026 ranges — re-check on publish day. Full bandsaw mills ship freight; check the listing's shipping terms before you order.

Tools · Guide 10

Best skid steer and tractor attachments

A skid steer or a compact tractor is only as useful as what you hang on the front - or the back. The machine is the expensive part. The attachments are where the work happens, and they are also where the affiliate money is: grapple buckets, pallet forks, augers and 3-point implements are all sold on Amazon in the $125-$5,000 range, they ship freight to your door, and at 3% a single grapple bucket sale pays $60-$90. This guide only lists attachments we could verify as actually listed on Amazon in November 2026. If we could not confirm the Amazon listing, it is not a pick.

One thing before the picks: fitment matters more than brand here. An attachment that does not match your machine's mount, hitch category, or hydraulic flow is a very expensive paperweight. There is a full "will it fit my machine?" section after the picks - read it before you order.

Buy it if…

  • You own a skid steer or compact tractor and you've checked fitment first — mount (SSQA vs pin-on), hitch category, and hydraulic flow. That check is what separates a workhorse from a very expensive paperweight.
  • You want the three that cover most jobs first: a pallet fork frame, a grapple bucket, and a ballast box — moving, grabbing, and lifting safely.
  • You checked the wear parts — tines, blades and cutting edges should be replaceable, with spares sold before you buy.

Skip it if…

  • You haven't checked your machine's flow rating — a grapple needs about 10–15 GPM, an auger 10–25 GPM, a brush cutter 12–21 GPM. Too little flow and the attachment stalls.
  • The attachment eats your lift capacity — a 970 lb grapple on a 2,200 lb loader leaves you 1,230 lb of actual lifting. Subtract the attachment weight first.
  • Your PTO horsepower doesn't match — a 72" tiller on a 25 HP tractor will bog down; a 37" tiller on a 50 HP tractor wastes the tractor.
The verdict

If you own one machine and want the most useful attachments first, buy in this order: a pallet fork frame, a grapple bucket, and a ballast box. Those three cover moving, grabbing, and lifting safely. After that, add the attachment that matches the job you actually do most - an auger for fencing, a tiller for food plots, a brush cutter for clearing. And before any of it, check your mount, your hitch category, and your hydraulic flow. The right attachment on the wrong machine is the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Will it fit my machine?

Skid steer quick attach (SSQA). Most modern skid steers and many compact tractor loaders use the universal skid steer quick attach (SSQA) - two levers, one plate, and the attachment locks on. If your machine has SSQA, every skid steer attachment in this guide fits. If it has a pin-on bucket or a brand-specific mount (John Deere hook-and-pin, Euro/Global), you need an adapter plate first - Titan sells one for John Deere hook-and-pin loaders for about $720.

3-point hitch categories. 3-point implements are sized by hitch category, not by brand. Category 1 covers most compact and sub-compact tractors from about 20 to 45 HP, with 7/8" lower link pins. Category 0 is for garden tractors under 20 HP, Category 2 for 40-100 HP utility tractors. Every 3-point pick in this guide is Category 1 unless stated otherwise. If you do not know your category, check your tractor's manual - it is printed there.

Hydraulic flow (GPM). Hydraulic attachments - grapples, augers, brush cutters - need enough auxiliary hydraulic flow. A grapple needs about 10-15 GPM, an auger 10-25 GPM, a brush cutter 12-21 GPM depending on size. Too little flow and the attachment stalls; too much and you can damage seals. Your machine's flow rating is in the manual and on the spec plate. Mini skid steers and sub-compacts are often low-flow - check before ordering anything hydraulic.

Weight vs lift capacity. An attachment's weight counts against your lift capacity. A 970 lb grapple on a loader rated for 2,200 lb leaves you 1,230 lb of actual lifting. Always subtract the attachment weight first, and add rear ballast when you lift heavy.

PTO and horsepower. PTO implements need a 540 RPM PTO and the right horsepower. A 72" tiller on a 25 HP tractor will bog down; a 37" tiller on a 50 HP tractor wastes the tractor. Match the implement's HP range to your tractor.

What actually matters

Build. Steel thickness and weld quality. Grapples and buckets live a hard life - 1/4" tines and a reinforced frame last, thin steel bends on the first rock.

Hydraulics. Cylinder count and PSI rating on grapples. Twin 3,000 PSI cylinders grip better and last longer than a single small cylinder.

Wear parts. Replaceable wear parts. Tines, blades and cutting edges should be replaceable - check that spares are sold before you buy.

Shipping. Freight and delivery. Most of these ship by freight, not parcel. Read the delivery terms: liftgate service, residential delivery fees, and whether you need a forklift or a second machine to unload.

Support. Warranty and parts support. Titan, AGT and the other brands in this guide sell parts direct - check that before buying a no-name attachment with no spares.

FAQs

Can I buy a skid steer attachment on Amazon and have it delivered to my house?Yes - most of the attachments in this guide are sold on Amazon and ship by freight to a residential address. Expect a freight delivery appointment and possibly a liftgate fee. Read the listing's delivery terms before you order.
Will a universal quick attach bucket fit my John Deere tractor?Only if your loader has the SSQA plate or you add an adapter. Many John Deere loaders use a hook-and-pin mount instead. Titan sells a hook-and-pin to SSQA adapter plate for about $720 - without it, SSQA attachments will not fit.
What size grapple do I need?Match the grapple width to your machine width and your lift capacity. A 48" grapple suits sub-compacts and mini skid steers; 72" suits full-size skid steers and 60-75 HP tractors. Subtract the grapple's weight from your lift capacity first.
Do I need rear ballast when using a grapple or pallet forks?Almost always, yes. A loaded grapple or a pallet of material on the front shifts the balance forward. A ballast box on the 3-point hitch - or a heavy rear implement - keeps the rear wheels planted.
Are these attachments really on Amazon, or do I have to call a dealer?Every pick in this guide was verified as listed on Amazon in November 2026. The machines in Guide 2 are a different story - most of those are dealer purchases, and the guide says so.

Prices are approximate November 2026 ranges — heavy equipment prices move and freight terms vary, so re-check on Amazon before you buy.

A $35,000 mini excavator is a dealer purchase - financing, delivery, service, warranty - not a click-to-cart item. So why write the guide? Because the person researching a $35,000 machine is the same person who buys a $2,500 grapple bucket, a $3,000 tiller, and $800 of pallet forks. Buy it if…

  • You've picked the size class first — horsepower is the headline, but lift capacity, hydraulic flow and weight matter more day to day.
  • There's a dealer within driving distance — a warranty is only as good as the dealer who does the work, and parts availability matters before the machine breaks.
  • You've budgeted for attachments on top of the machine price — a grapple, forks and a ballast box are where the money goes next.

Skip it if…

  • You're expecting to click-buy a name-brand machine on Amazon — Kubota, Bobcat and Cat machines are dealer-only. Only the small AGT imports sell through Amazon.
  • You haven't rented first — a weekend rental (about $240–$350 a day) tells you more about what size you need than any spec sheet.
  • Resale matters and you're buying the cheapest badge — Deere, Kubota and Cat hold roughly 55–66% at five years; TYM and Mahindra cost less up front and keep less.
The verdict

Buy the machine from a dealer, and buy the attachments online. That is the whole strategy in one sentence. The tractor or excavator is a $15,000-$45,000 relationship with a dealer - financing, service, warranty, resale. The grapple bucket, the pallet forks, the auger, and the tiller are $125-$5,000 purchases that Amazon ships to your door, and they are the same attachments whether the machine came from Deere or Kubota. Start with Guide 1, the attachments guide, outfit the machine you have or the one you are about to buy, and use this guide to make sure the machine itself is the right size before you sign anything.

How to buy a machine (the honest version)

Dealer machines. Get three out-the-door quotes in writing. List price, dealer price, and out-the-door price are three different numbers. Freight, setup, tax, and attachments can add $1,500-$4,000 to a tractor and far more to an excavator.

Warranty. Ask what the warranty covers and who does the work. A warranty is only as good as the dealer within driving distance. Check parts availability before you buy, not after it breaks.

Financing. 0% financing is common on new compact tractors and mini excavators. Run the numbers - a 0% deal on a $25,000 machine often beats a cash discount on a used one.

Amazon import machines. For the AGT import machines: they ship freight, you need a phone number for the carrier, and you will assemble and adjust the machine yourself. There is no local dealer. Budget for your own tools, fluids, and time.

Try first. Rent before you buy. A weekend rental of a mini excavator or mini skid steer (about $240-$350 a day) tells you more about what size you need than any spec sheet.

Budget for attachments. Whatever machine you buy, the attachments in Guide 1 are where the money goes next - budget for a grapple, forks, and a ballast box on top of the machine price.

What actually matters

Specs that matter. Horsepower is the headline, but lift capacity, hydraulic flow, and weight matter more day to day. A 25 HP tractor that lifts 1,000 lb is more useful than a 30 HP tractor that lifts 700 lb.

Dealer network. A machine with a dealer 20 minutes away beats a better machine with a dealer 3 hours away. Check dealer density before brand loyalty.

Resale. Deere, Kubota and Cat hold value best - roughly 55-66% retention at five years. TYM and Mahindra cost less up front and keep less at resale. Both can be the right call; know which one you are making.

Import vs name brand. A 1-ton import mini excavator is a homeowner machine. A 2-ton Kubota or Bobcat is a commercial machine. Do not compare them on price alone - compare them on what happens when something breaks.

Size classes. Mini excavators: dig depth, tail swing (zero tail swing fits in tight spots), and whether a thumb is included. Mini skid steers: rated operating capacity, track vs wheels, and stand-on vs sit-down.

FAQs

Can I really buy a mini excavator on Amazon?Yes - but only the small import ones. AGT sells 1-ton mini excavators and mini skid steers through Amazon for $5,000-$13,000, freight-delivered. Full-size Kubota, Bobcat, and Cat machines are dealer-only; Amazon does not sell them.
How much does a compact tractor cost in 2026?A new sub-compact with a loader runs about $12,500-$24,500 depending on brand - TYM and Mahindra at the low end, Kubota and John Deere at the high end. Used machines commonly list $9,500-$20,000. Always get an out-the-door quote; the brochure price is not the price.
Should I buy new or used?New buys you warranty, 0% financing, and known history. Used buys you 30-50% off for a machine with a few hundred hours. For a first machine, a low-hour used unit from a dealer - with a warranty - is often the smartest money.
What size mini excavator do I need?For footings, trenches, drainage and stumps on a home property, a 1.7-2 ton machine (Kubota U17, Bobcat E20) is the sweet spot. Go bigger only if you dig deep foundations or lift heavy pipe regularly - and remember you have to trailer it.
Is a mini skid steer worth it for a homeowner?If you move material, grade, dig, or clear land more than a few weekends a year, yes - a mini skid steer with a bucket, forks and an auger replaces a wheelbarrow, a shovel, and a lot of weekends. Rent one first for a weekend and see how much you get done.

Tools · Guide 12

Chainsaw safety gear and firewood tools

A chainsaw does not care how experienced you are. The chain moves at around 45 mph, and the difference between a bad day and a story you tell later is usually a $70 pair of chaps and a helmet you bothered to put on. This guide is the full kit: what to wear before you pull the starter cord, and the hand tools that move and split the wood once it is down — 41 picks across nine sections.

Everything here is sold on Amazon, with the ratings that actually matter — NRR for hearing, ANSI Z87.1 for eyes, UL/ASTM F1897 for chaps, NIOSH N95/P100 for lungs.

As an Amazon Associate, ShedWorks earns from qualifying purchases.

Quick picks — Log splitting hand tools

A splitting axe splits by speed and wedge geometry; a maul splits by weight. For most homeowners splitting under 10 cords a year, a 36-inch splitting axe is the right tool, and a maul plus a wedge is what you reach for when a round will not crack. Never drive a steel wedge with the poll of an ordinary axe — use a maul or a sledgehammer.

Hookaroons, pickaroons and log handling

A hookaroon (also spelled hookeroon) is a long handle with a hooked point that lets you grab, drag, roll and stack logs without bending over and putting your hands near the load. A pickaroon is the same idea with a sharper spike. Log tongs carry two logs at once; a timberjack lifts a log off the ground so you can cut it without the chain hitting dirt.

Chainsaw chaps

Chaps are the single most important piece of chainsaw safety gear. The protective fibers inside jam the chain sprocket and stop the chain in milliseconds on contact. Look for UL classification to ASTM F1897 — if the listing does not name a standard, the protection is unverified. Most homeowner chaps are rated for a single chain contact: after a hit, replace them even if they look fine.

Hearing protection

A gas chainsaw runs around 100–110 dB. Hearing damage starts at 85 dB over a workday, and it does not heal. NRR is the lab rating — real-world protection is roughly half the NRR, so aim for 25 dB NRR or better for chainsaw work. Electronic muffs let you hear conversation and warnings; Bluetooth muffs let you hear music or podcasts on long jobs.

Masks and respirators

Sawdust is 5–30 microns; the fine dust that hangs in the air after sanding is smaller and stays in your lungs. A cloth mask is not protection. N95 filters at least 95% of airborne particles; P100 filters 99.97% and resists oil-based particles. For a quick cut, a valved N95 disposable. For a full day of sanding or splitting in a dusty barn, a reusable half mask with P100 filters.

Buy the gear if…

  • You run a chainsaw at all — chaps and a helmet system first. They protect the parts a chain can reach in a second, and most homeowner chainsaw injuries happen to occasional users.
  • The listing names its standard — UL/ASTM F1897 for chaps, ANSI Z87.1 for eyes, NRR 25 dB or better for ears, NIOSH N95 or P100 for lungs.
  • You're starting from zero — the Husqvarna Classic PPE kit bundles chaps, helmet and gloves for about $150–$165, cheaper than the parts.

Skip it if…

  • No standard is named on the chaps — no standard named, no buy. The protection is unverified.
  • You're planning to cut in regular work gloves — plain leather protects against splinters, not a chain. Chainsaw gloves have stopper fabric for cutting; leather is for splitting and stacking.
  • Your chaps already took a chain hit — chaps are single-use protection. Replace them after a contact even if they look fine.
The verdict

1. Chaps and a helmet system first — they protect the parts a chain can reach in a second. The Husqvarna PPE kit covers both plus gloves for about $150–$165. 2. Eye and ear protection next — glasses and muffs are cheap and you will use them every time. 3. Gloves and a mask — chainsaw gloves for cutting, leather gloves for splitting, an N95 for dust. 4. A trauma kit in the truck — you hope never to open it. 5. Then the hand tools: a splitting axe, a hookaroon, a wedge, and a timberjack. The wood does not care how fast you split it, but your back will notice the right tools.

What actually matters — the ratings

Head weight. 6 lb axe for speed, 8 lb maul for brute force on knotty wood.

Handle. FiberComp/fiberglass shrugs off overstrikes; hickory feels better but can break on a bad miss.

Steel. forged heads hardened to about 45–55 HRC hold an edge without chipping.

Wedges. 4–6 lb, finned or fluted sides resist binding; always drive with a maul or sledge.

Certification. UL classification to ASTM F1897 (the -20 version is the current standard) or OSHA 1910.266 compliance. No standard named, no buy.

Style. apron chaps cover the front of the legs and are cooler; wrap-around chaps cover 360 degrees and protect calves when limbing.

Fit. measure your inseam and waist — chaps that are too long are a trip hazard.

Layers. 5–8 protective layers is normal for homeowner chaps; more layers is not automatically better if the fit is wrong.

NRR 25 dB or better for chainsaw work; 30 dB is the top end for passive muffs.

Electronic muffs trade a few dB of NRR for the ability to hear warnings and conversation — worth it when you work with a helper.

Fit matters more than the number. glasses, hair and a bad seal all cut real protection. If the cups do not seal, the rating is fiction.

Chaps. UL classification to ASTM F1897. No standard named, no buy.

Helmets. ANSI Z89.1 for the hard hat shell; mesh visors do not fog, clear visors keep rain out.

Glasses. ANSI Z87.1 minimum, Z87.1+ for high-velocity impact; anti-fog if you wear a mask.

Hearing. NRR 25 dB or better for chainsaws; real protection is roughly half the lab NRR.

Masks. NIOSH N95 minimum for sawdust; P100 for heavy dust and old buildings.

Gloves. EN381-7 / EN ISO 11393-4 for chainsaw protection; plain leather for splitting and stacking.

Boots. ASTM F2413 steel toe minimum; chainsaw-rated boots with cut protection exist but are overkill for occasional homeowners.

FAQs

Do I really need chaps for occasional use?Yes. Most chainsaw injuries to homeowners happen on the leg, and they happen to occasional users more than pros. Chaps are the cheapest serious protection you can buy.
Apron chaps or wrap-around chaps?Apron chaps cover the front of the legs and run cooler. Wrap-around chaps cover 360 degrees and protect your calves when you limb on uneven ground. If you only buck rounds on flat ground, apron is fine.
Can I use my regular work gloves with a chainsaw?For splitting and stacking, yes. For cutting, wear chainsaw gloves — the stopper fabric on the back of the hand is what jams the chain. Regular leather will not stop it.
Do chaps work more than once?No. They are rated for a single chain contact. After a hit, replace them even if they look fine — the protective fibers inside are spent.
What should be in a chainsaw first aid kit?A real tourniquet (CAT or SOFTT-W), compressed gauze for packing wounds, an Israeli pressure bandage, and a phone. Learn to apply the tourniquet before you need it — a three-minute video could save a life. Never cut alone without telling someone where you are.

As an Amazon Associate, ShedWorks earns from qualifying purchases.

Why a home welder pays for itself — Josh's story

Josh does a lot of welding, and he has manufactured his own log splitter and some of his own equipment. That is the whole point of a home welder: once you can cut steel, join it and grind it smooth, you stop buying things other people built and start building what you actually need. A log splitter is a real piece of equipment — frame, wedge, hydraulics, hitch — and building one yourself saves real money and leaves you with a machine you can repair yourself forever.

That is the lens this guide is written through. Every welder below is judged on whether it can do real garage fabrication — brackets, repairs, trailers, splitter frames, shop equipment — not just lay a pretty bead on a coupon.

One brand in this guide is a first-hand recommendation, not a research pick. Josh runs Hobart welders himself, and his words are: "I run Hobart welders myself — they work great and they don't cost what a Miller does." The Hobart Handler 140, Handler 190, Handler 210 MVP and Multi-Handler 200 below are his picks. Everything else in this guide is a research roundup: we checked specs, prices and reviews, but we have not run those machines ourselves.

Which welder for what — MIG vs flux-core vs stick vs TIG

MIG (with gas) is the easiest way to learn and the cleanest for garage fabrication — thin steel, sheet metal, brackets, furniture. Flux-core is MIG without the gas bottle: more spatter and smoke, but it works outdoors in the wind and costs less to start. Stick is the farm welder — it burns through rust, paint and dirty steel outdoors, and it is the cheapest way to weld thick steel. TIG is the precision process: thin steel, stainless and (with an AC machine) aluminum, but it is the slowest to learn and the most expensive per amp.

  • MIG / flux-core: First welder, garage fabrication, learn fast: MIG or flux-core (Hobart Handler 140 or Forney 261).
  • Stick: Outdoor repair, rusty steel, thick plate, no gas bottle: stick (Hobart Stickmate 160).
  • TIG: Thin steel, stainless, aluminum, pretty welds: TIG, and only an AC/DC machine welds aluminum.
  • Multi-process: One machine to try everything: multi-process (YesWelder MIG-205DS PRO or ARCCAPTAIN MIG200).
  • Plasma: Cutting plate and shapes fast: plasma cutter — pairs with any welder, replaces the cutting torch for most shop work.

Power matters too. A 120V machine plugs into any garage outlet and welds up to about 1/4 in. steel. A dual-voltage 120/240V machine starts on 120V and grows into a 240V circuit later — buy dual voltage if you can, because a 240V circuit is the single best upgrade a home shop ever gets.

TIG welders

TIG gives the cleanest, most controlled weld of any home process — thin steel, stainless, and aluminum. The trap: most affordable 'TIG' machines, including the TIG mode on multi-process welders, are DC-only. DC welds steel and stainless but cannot weld aluminum. Aluminum needs AC, so confirm 'AC/DC' on the spec sheet before you buy.

Buy it if: you want to weld aluminum without spending over $1,000. Skip it if: you only weld steel — a DC machine costs half as much.

Multi-process welders

One box that runs MIG, flux-core, stick and (usually DC) lift TIG. The shortest path from an unopened box to your first decent bead — and the best choice if you are not sure which process you will end up using most. Watch the box contents: the cheapest combos quietly leave out the TIG torch, the gas regulator or the electrode holder you actually need on day one.

Plasma cutters

A plasma cutter is the fastest, cleanest way to cut sheet metal and plate steel in a home shop. It pairs with any welder and replaces the cutting torch for most shop work. You need an air compressor — every cutter here needs clean, dry compressed air. Pilot arc matters: it lets the torch fire without touching the metal, so it cuts through rust and paint without stalling.

Plasma cutter

Buy it if: you regularly cut 1/2 in. plate and want a cutter that lasts. Skip it if: you only cut thin sheet occasionally — the CUT50DP does that for half the money.

Auto-darkening welding helmets

A helmet is not optional and it is not the place to save $20. Look for 4 arc sensors, a 1/1/1/1 optical clarity rating, a shade range that goes down to 8 (OSHA's minimum for TIG under 150A), and a switching speed of 1/20,000 second or faster. True-color lenses are worth it — they correct the old lime-green tint so you can actually see the puddle.

Wire, rods and consumables

Consumables are the running cost of welding, and cheap wire is a false economy — inconsistent wire feeds badly, spatters more and makes ugly welds. Buy name-brand wire and rods; the price difference per pound is small and the frustration difference is large.

These are real products, but we could NOT confirm a reliable Amazon listing for them in November 2026. They are NOT picks — do not link them to Amazon. Buy them from the maker's own store or a welding dealer.

  • PrimeWeld TIG225X: PrimeWeld TIG225X — 225A AC/DC TIG, about $869. PrimeWeld sells it direct from its own store; no current Amazon listing turned up in a November 2026 check. A great machine, but buy it from PrimeWeld.
  • Miller Multimatic 215 / 220: Miller Multimatic 215 — 230A multi-process, about $2,183. Miller welders are sold through welding-supply dealers, not Amazon. Same for the Multimatic 220 AC/DC. Buy from a Miller dealer.
  • Hypertherm Powermax30 XP: Hypertherm Powermax30 XP — the benchmark plasma cutter, about $1,500+. A dealer and welding-supply item; third-party Amazon listings exist at big markups. Buy from a Hypertherm dealer.
  • Lincoln Square Wave 205: Lincoln Square Wave 205 TIG — about $1,530. A dealer-channel Lincoln machine; buy from a Lincoln dealer, not Amazon.
  • ESAB Sentinel helmets: ESAB Sentinel A70 / A60 helmets — excellent helmets (the A60 has the largest viewing area in its class at 13 sq in.), but Amazon stock and pricing were inconsistent in November 2026. Check the live listing before publishing as a pick.

Buy a home welder if…

  • You want to stop buying things other people built — Josh manufactured his own log splitter and some of his own equipment, and a machine you built is a machine you can repair yourself forever.
  • You do real garage fabrication — brackets, repairs, trailers, splitter frames, shop equipment — not just practice beads.
  • You can buy dual voltage — a 120V machine starts anywhere, and a dual-voltage machine grows into a 240V circuit later, the single best upgrade a home shop ever gets.

Skip it if…

  • You want to weld aluminum with a DC-only TIG machine — it physically cannot do it. Aluminum needs AC; check for 'AC/DC' on the spec sheet before you buy.
  • The budget box leaves out what you need on day one — the cheapest combos quietly skip the TIG torch, the gas regulator or the electrode holder.
  • You're about to link a Miller welder or a PrimeWeld TIG225X to Amazon — we could not confirm reliable Amazon listings for them; they're dealer / direct-store machines (see the note at the end of this guide).
The verdict

If you are starting from nothing, buy in this order:

1. Helmet: Helmet first — Lincoln VIKING 3350 if you can, YesWelder LYG-M800H if you cannot. Never strike an arc without one.

2. Welder: Hobart Handler 140 — Josh's pick, and the machine you will still be using in ten years. Add the Forney 261 only if the budget is truly under $200.

3. Gloves and jacket: Tillman 50 gloves and a Revco BSX FR jacket. Skin protection is not optional.

4. Grinder and wire: DeWalt DWE402 grinder and a 10 lb spool of Hobart flux-core wire. Prep and consumables.

5. Respirator and blanket: 3M 7502 respirator and a welding blanket. Cheap insurance for your lungs and your shop.

6. Plasma cutter and table: PrimeWeld CUT50DP plasma cutter and a DeWalt welding table. The cutting and the work surface that turn a welder into a fabrication shop.

7. TIG, later: AHP AlphaTIG 203Xi — only when you are ready for thin steel, stainless and aluminum, and only after the MIG setup is paid for.

And the reason any of this is worth buying: a welder pays for itself the first time you build something instead of buying it. Josh built his own log splitter and his own equipment. That is not a hobby project — that is a machine that splits wood every winter, built for the cost of steel and a weekend of welding. Start with the helmet, the Hobart and the gloves, and build from there.

What actually matters

Duty cycle. Duty cycle is the real spec. 20% at 90A means 2 minutes welding out of every 10 at that setting before the machine needs to cool. A 60% duty cycle machine welds three times as long.

Dual voltage. Dual voltage (120/240V) is the single best upgrade path. A 120V-only machine is a dead end once you get a 240V circuit; a dual-voltage machine grows with the shop.

Amps. Amps decide thickness. Roughly: 140A handles up to 3/16 in. steel, 200A handles up to 3/8 in. on 240V. Buy more amps than you think you need — you will use them.

Transformer vs inverter. A transformer machine (Lincoln Tombstone) is heavy and nearly indestructible. An inverter machine is light and portable but has more electronics to fail. Both weld fine.

Support. Miller and Lincoln have dealer networks and real service. Import brands (YesWelder, ARCCAPTAIN, Amico) have online-only support and lower prices. That is the trade, and it is worth knowing before you buy.

Spool gun. A spool gun is how a MIG machine welds aluminum — soft aluminum wire will not feed through a normal MIG gun. If aluminum is on your list, check spool-gun compatibility.

Box contents. Check what is actually in the box. Budget multi-process machines sometimes leave out the TIG torch, the gas regulator or the electrode holder — and those cost real money to add.

Welding safety — the short version

Eyes. Helmet on before you strike an arc, every time. Flash burn feels like sand in your eyes and it hurts for a day.

Skin. Gloves, jacket and long sleeves — UV from an arc burns skin like sunburn, and spatter burns worse.

Lungs. Ventilation or a respirator. Welding fume is the hazard most home welders underestimate, and galvanized steel fume is genuinely dangerous — grind the zinc off first and weld it outdoors.

Fire. Move combustibles at least 35 feet from the work and keep a fire watch for at least 30 minutes after you finish — OSHA's welding standard, and the rule that saves shops.

Electricity and explosions. Ground the table or the workpiece, keep cables out of the way, and never weld on a closed container or a fuel tank.

Ears. Ear protection when grinding. A grinder is louder than a welder, and hearing damage is permanent.

FAQs

What is the best welder for a complete beginner?A 120V flux-core or MIG machine: the Forney Easy Weld 261 if your budget is under $200, or the Hobart Handler 140 if you want to buy once. Both run on a standard garage outlet and both will teach you the fundamentals without a gas bottle.
Do I need a 240V circuit to weld at home?No — every 120V machine in this guide welds up to about 1/4 in. steel on a normal outlet. A 240V circuit matters when you want to weld thicker steel or run a bigger machine, and it is the best single upgrade a home shop can make. Buy a dual-voltage machine now and add the circuit later.
Can a cheap welder really weld, or is it a toy?A cheap welder from a real brand really welds. The Forney 261 and the YesWelder machines lay real beads on real steel — the trade is duty cycle, wire drive quality and support, not whether the weld holds. The machines to avoid are the no-name boxes with no reviews and no warranty.
MIG or stick for farm and outdoor repair?Stick. It burns through rust and paint, works in the wind, and needs no gas bottle. The Hobart Stickmate 160 is the pick. MIG is better in the shop on clean steel; stick is better outside on the real world.
What does a home welder actually cost to get started?A complete starter setup — machine, helmet, gloves, jacket, wire and a grinder — runs about $400 to $700 with a budget machine, or $800 to $1,200 with a Hobart or Lincoln. The machine is only about half the cost; the protective gear is the other half, and it is not optional.
Can I weld aluminum with a cheap TIG welder?Only with an AC/DC machine. Most affordable TIG machines are DC-only, which welds steel and stainless but cannot weld aluminum — aluminum needs AC to clean the oxide layer. The AHP AlphaTIG 203Xi is the cheapest AC/DC TIG in this guide that genuinely welds aluminum.

Prices are approximate November 2026 ranges — welder prices move with sales and coupons, so re-check on publish day before buying.

Size your power station

Thirty seconds of math beats a return shipping label. Pick the thing you most need to keep running.

Backup runtime calculator

Pick an appliance (or type in its watts from the label on the back), set how many hours of actual run time you need, and we'll work out the battery size — with a 20% cushion, because no battery gives up every last watt-hour.

1,440 Wh

150W × 8 hours = 1,200 Wh, plus a 20% cushion.

Shop the ~1.5–2 kWh class (EcoFlow Delta / Bluetti AC200 class) — or an expandable unit you can grow.

From my own house · Pekin, Illinois

What I learned building my own solar system

I started small, and I believe it was a good learning experience — but not the right way to go if your goal is powering a house. Here's the road I took, so you can skip the expensive parts of it.

  • 12V
    The learning systemA small 12-volt setup that would power a refrigerator. It taught me how solar, charging and batteries actually work — and it taught me its limits just as fast.
  • 24V
    The step upA 24-volt system that powered part of the house. Better in every way — and still not enough for the whole job.
  • 48V
    The best idea yetA 48-volt system with 25 kWh of battery. An EG4 12000XP inverter runs my house and garage at the same time, with five 100Ah 48V server-rack batteries that all communicate together. The system basically runs without intervention.

On the roof: about 30 panels, roughly a 7 kW array, charging the batteries every day. Most days, I hardly ever have power on from the electric company at all.

~30panels on the roof
~7 kWtotal array size
25 kWhbattery storage
5 × 100Ah48V server-rack batteries

Skip straight to 48V

If you think you'll ever power a house, don't buy your system three times like I did. 12V teaches, 24V tempts, 48V is where whole-house systems live — higher voltage, lower current, less loss, real inverter choices.

Buy the battery once

Batteries are the expensive part, and a small one can't grow into a big one. My five rack batteries talk to each other and act as one 25 kWh bank — buy expandable, or buy the size you actually need the first time. Same rule applies to portable power stations.

Buy smart, not fast

I bought my panels used from Santan Solar — they're running out of used panels now, but new panels aren't that expensive anymore. The batteries came from Black Friday deals at 40% off. The gear is the expensive part; timing is free money.

Questions I get asked

Who writes ShedWorks?

Josh, a homeowner in Pekin, Illinois. The tool and mower guides come from the same homework I'd do for my own garage; the solar content comes from a system I designed, bought and built myself — 12V to 24V to the 48V, 25 kWh setup that now runs my house and garage.

How do the picks make money?

ShedWorks is an Amazon Associate site: if you buy through a product link here, the site earns a small commission at no extra cost to you. That's the whole business model, which is why the guides say "skip it" when skipping is the right answer — a returned or regretted purchase helps nobody.

Why do the guides push "battery platforms" so hard?

Because the battery is the system. One platform's packs run your drill, trimmer, blower and lights for a decade. Three platforms means three chargers, three sets of spare batteries, and three times the cost. It's the same lesson as my solar build: buy the battery once.

Can a portable power station replace a system like yours?

No — and it's not trying to. A 1–2 kWh station covers a fridge, lights and phones through an outage. Whole-house backup took me ~7 kW of panels, 25 kWh of batteries and a 12,000W-class inverter. Start with the station if that's your need; just buy an expandable one if you think you'll grow.

Are the prices exact?

No — they're approximate street prices as of November 2026, shown so you can budget and spot a real sale. Tool and battery gear swings a lot around holiday sales; check the current price before you buy, and remember the Black Friday rule from my battery purchase: patience is worth about 40%.
